content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are a widespread health issue, affecting over 7 million individuals globally. While many people experience only one episode in their lifetime and respond well to standard antibiotic treatments, a significant subset of the population—approximately 15% to 25% of adults and children—suffers from chronic, symptomatic UTIs. Certain groups, such as those with compromised immune systems or chronic kidney disease, are at an even higher risk of developing these infections. D-mannose is a naturally occurring sugar that is part of normal human metabolism and is present in most diets. Its mechanism of action involves preventing bacteria, particularly uropathogenic Escherichia coli (E. coli), from adhering to the cells lining the urinary tract (uroepithelial cells). By blocking bacterial adhesion and invasion, D-mannose facilitates the elimination of these pathogens through urination. Early pilot studies in both animals and humans have tested concentrated forms of D-mannose, administered in doses ranging from 200 mg to 2–3 g, and have suggested potential efficacy in reducing UTI symptoms or recurrence. However, while the anti-adhesive properties of D-mannose are well-documented, only a limited number of small pilot studies and clinical trials have been conducted to evaluate its effectiveness. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of D-mannose in preventing and treating UTIs in both adults and children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to February 22, 2022. This database includes studies identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP) Search Portal, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the effects of D-mannose, in any formulation or combination, for the prevention or treatment of UTIs in males and females of all ages and in any setting (including perioperative contexts) were included. Titles, abstracts, and full texts were independently reviewed by the authors to determine eligibility. Data extraction was performed independently by two authors using a standardized form, and the methodological quality of the included studies was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Seven RCTs involving 719 participants were included in the review. These participants were adult males and females with either acute cystitis or a history of recurrent UTIs (defined as at least two episodes in six months or three episodes in 12 months, either symptomatic or asymptomatic). The studies included two focused on prevention, four on both prevention and treatment (including two perioperative studies and one involving individuals with multiple sclerosis), and one on treatment alone. The duration of the studies ranged from 15 days to six months. The studies varied significantly in terms of D-mannose dosage and treatment protocols, making it impossible to perform meta-analyses. Individual studies provided no clear evidence to determine whether D-mannose is more or less effective than other treatments in preventing or treating UTIs. For example, one study involving 205 participants compared D-mannose (2 g) to no treatment and found uncertain effects on symptomatic and bacteriuria-confirmed UTIs, with the evidence rated as very low certainty. Another study with 206 participants compared D-mannose (2 g) to the antibiotic nitrofurantoin (50 mg) and also found very low certainty evidence. Similarly, D-mannose combined with herbal supplements showed uncertain effects when compared to no treatment in a study of 40 participants. In another trial, D-mannose (500 mg) combined with N-acetylcysteine and Morinda citrifolia fruit extract was compared to the antibiotic prulifloxacin (400 mg) in 75 participants, with similarly uncertain results. Adverse events associated with D-mannose were infrequent and poorly reported, with none classified as serious. The most commonly reported side effects were mild, such as diarrhea and vaginal burning. Overall, the quality of the evidence was poor, with most studies judged to have a high or unclear risk of bias across multiple domains. The data were sparse, addressing only a limited number of outcomes, and the GRADE evaluation rated the evidence as very low certainty due to serious limitations in study design, execution, and small sample sizes. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of D-mannose for the prevention or treatment of UTIs in any population. This review underscores the critical lack of high-quality RCTs investigating the efficacy of D-mannose as an alternative treatment for UTIs. Despite the high prevalence of UTIs—affecting 50% of women at least once in their lifetime—and the growing concern of global antimicrobial resistance, few studies have adequately tested this potential intervention. Future research should prioritize conducting a single, well-powered RCT comparing D-mannose to a placebo to provide more definitive evidence.
